The finite element method (FEM) leads to sparse matrix systems with O(N) storage requirements, advantageous over integral equation methods with O(N²) storage.
Absorbing boundary conditions (ABCs) are approximate local boundary conditions applied on artificial mesh truncation surfaces to simulate open domains.
Exact boundary conditions on truncation surfaces can cause uniqueness problems and partly full system matrices, reducing scalability.
Edge-based vector finite elements avoid spurious solutions common in nodal basis formulations for electromagnetic problems.
The dissertation includes formulations for 2D and 3D scalar and vector finite elements with various element shapes: triangles, rectangles, tetrahedra, and hexahedra.
Eigenvalue computations for empty and dielectric-filled metallic cavities validate the FEM formulation.
Radar cross-section (RCS) patterns computed with FEM-ABC match well with analytical and method of moments (MoM) results for various shapes.
Optimization includes sparse matrix storage, preconditioned iterative solvers, and parallelization on KSR1 and Intel iPSC/80 architectures.
Block ILU preconditioning reduces the number of iterations required for convergence compared to diagonal preconditioning.
Conformal ABCs are developed to apply absorbing conditions on curved mesh termination surfaces, reducing computational domain size.
The finite element mesh must be extended sufficiently far from the scatterer for ABCs to be effective.
The dissertation addresses both closed domain (bounded) and open domain (unbounded) electromagnetic problems.
The Galerkin method is used to derive finite element equations from Maxwell's equations.
Spurious modes arise from improper basis functions and are mitigated by using edge-based vector shape functions.
Parallelization analysis includes communication overhead and load balancing for sparse matrix-vector multiplication.

The finite element-ABC method can handle composite geometries with metallic and dielectric sections.
Higher-order hierarchical basis functions for tetrahedral elements are presented.
The absorbing boundary conditions are designed to absorb the lowest order terms of the field expansion at the truncation boundary.
The dissertation includes detailed numerical results and comparisons for various benchmark electromagnetic scattering problems.
